synopsis: Physically based rendering uses light and material physics to compute sensor observations, but non-visual material behaviour cannot be inferred from RGB appearance and must be specified by wavelength or sensor band [f12939, f3713, f3926, f4298]. Lidar needs wavelength-specific reflectance and BRDF, radar needs permittivity, conductivity, roughness and multipath, thermal sensing needs emissivity, and cameras need physically based materials and spectral response; modelling darkness additionally requires calibrated noise, exposure and image processing [f12940, f12941, f12942, f12943, f4691]. Material-aware radar interaction and multipath improve sim-to-real behaviour over simple one-hit ray casting, while wet-ground lidar effects and difficult wet or dirty BRDFs show why surface realism matters [f5054, f4719, f4723]. ASAM OpenMATERIAL 3D version 1.0.0, dated April 2025, lets assets carry camera-, lidar- and radar-relevant properties, but excludes weather and lighting; planned version 1.1.0 adds better conductivity modelling and measured-reflectance-to-BRDF conversion [f12945, f12946, f3924]. No job-site measurement campaign in an OpenMATERIAL-type format was found for the listed materials, so the validation programme must measure or estimate properties itself—a larger schedule item than computing power, despite some camera and basic lidar simulations running in real time or faster [f4383, f12951, f4926]. The corpus retains a methodological tension between measured physics-first realism and learned models that reproduce observed output distributions, while warning that erroneous simulated reflectance and radar cross-section can compromise machine-learning training data [f4327, f7092].
